paragraphs: What do we mean by commissioning?
Foundations of good practice
Commissioning development offered through the PSTA draws from the good practice model of the eight aspects of commissioning.  Developed for the LGA and Partners in Care and Health​
What is the commissioning compass?
The compass is:
A system assessment tool for change
A framework to hold in mind – not a maturity model
Helps you see where change is possible
Reveals what holds your system back
Helps identify your best leverage points for change
What do we mean by system?

When you are commissioning for outcomes, you are connected to a large network of stakeholders, including citizens, communities, organisations, partners and providers.  All of this interconnecting network is your system. It makes up the complex whole.
What is the commissioning compass?
We help you to assess your system and give you a sense of direction about how you can plan to improve.
The goal - helping you navigate complexity and impact on outcomes for people and place
We have learned from practice in real places.
We engaged 60 practitioners in collaboration with the Local Government Association.​
We have formally tested in three councils – whole council, adult social care, children's services. ​
We have developed the PSTA's Commissioning Academies (insert link) around the framework of the aspects of the Compass.
What is the commissioning compass?

The commissioning compass enables you to take a strategic view of commissioning.  It lifts you out of just considering the commissioning process (although we cover that too), encouraging you to ask yourself deep, reflective questions, and exploring your context. It helps you see and understand where the pushes and pulls are and identify strengths and areas for improvement.
You can use the compass just for yourself.  Or as a tool for development with your team, across your department or organisation.
It works best with partners as part of a development process, enabling you to really stretch up into whole system working for wellbeing.
At the heart of this assessment is how you, as a strategic commissioner, work with complexity.
What is the commissioning compass?
To use the system assessment, first, you assess your system using our 'eight aspects' of commissioning model. These aspects help you to:
Appreciate how commissioning works now​
Identify where you can focus to unlock change​
See the full picture – not a single model​ or perspective
Begin (or continue) a developmental journey
Once you understand your system, use your current position, constraints, and enablers to create an action plan and to select the correct 'commissioning approach'.
Only go into as much detail as you have time for, and as is useful!
The Public Service Transformation Academy

The Public Service Transformation Academy is a not-for-profit social enterprise, with RedQuadrant as the lead partner. We were founded in 2016 to take over the Cabinet Office's 'Commissioning Academy' programme. Today, we deliver training, consultancy and transformation.
Our mission is to drive better outcomes for people and communities by developing the local, civil, social and health sectors’ capabilities to collaborate, innovate and lead.

The founders of this academy share some core beliefs: That most of the problems the public sector and society is dealing with have a significant underlying level of complexity. This complexity differs – it can arise from having to deal with multiple stakeholders, from complex citizen needs, from a need for cultural or behavioural change, or from a complex system of organisations that need to work together. Often, all these sources contribute to the complexity at the same time.
You can catch up on our latest activity, join our courses, and join our newsletter by following this link: https://link.redquadrant.com/m/PSTAOffers
Commissioning Academy

Set up as a flagship development programme by the Cabinet Office, this unique programme is focused on developing your skills and experience as a commissioner.​It brings together commissioners from across the system – often police, local government, adult social care, children's services, national bodies and many more. ​

We don't focus on rote learning or memorisation – you learn through doing in our action learning approach. Apply your learning to real challenges from your system in a hundred day plan to drive real change.​
Instructions for using the Commissioning Compass system assessment
Remember, only use as much of the assessment as makes sense for you in your situation.

The tool is intentionally wide-ranging to encompass strategic whole system working and commissioning tactics and processes. But it also takes you through a change process in each 'aspect’ of commissioning.

The temptation is to start at the top, 'whole system working' this aspect is rightly aspirational.  You may want to start at the foundational 'aspects'.  These then assess your system readiness for the stretch to the more aspirational 'aspects'

As an example. You may have good relationships in your system, but this is undermined by your capacity and capability. You may have good information and insight, but this is undermined by making room to make a difference. It is important to strengthen your system from the bottom up.
There are six steps to carrying out the full exercise:
Introducing the Commissioning Compass - eight aspects

The system assessment is structured around the eight 'aspects' of commissioning - An aspect is a part or feature of the total complexity of strategic commissioning.  Each aspect looks through a different lens.  Capturing therefore a wider perspective than traditionally captured in commissioning cycles or definitions.
Four of the aspects are more systems and outcome-based:​
Aspect 1 Whole system design: Work as one place to support and enable wellbeing, sustainability and mutual support.
Key question: Are we making a place that helps everyone live life well?​
Aspect 2 Relationships and organisation across the system: Everyone focused on achieving shared goals with aligned incentives and funding
Key question: Is everyone working together coherently across our place?​

Aspect 3 Capacity, capability, and confidence: Shape markets, provision, and delivery of all those (place, assets, VCFSE, employees, families, friends, carers, neighbours, community, etc) who enable people can live their lives well
Key question: Are we building the ability to meet or prevent needs, across all sectors?​
Aspect 4 Citizen, place, and outcome centred: Citizens in charge of their own outcomes, with success measured by people’s views on whether and to what extent they can live their lives well
Key question: Is the work led by the people or place who need it, and measured according to the outcomes they get?​
The other four are foundational pillars: ​
Aspect 5 Information, insight, and innovation: Commissioning approach that focusses on innovation and creativity and based on robust information / insight
Key question: Is the work led by the people or place who need it, and measured according to the outcomes they get?​
Aspect 6 Making room to make a difference: Meeting, interpreting, and actively shaping the policy and legal requirements that we have to work within
Key question: Do we understand and shape the law and policy we are working with? ​
Aspect 7 Commissioning process: Technically excellent, clear, and robust arrangements
Key question: Do we have a strong, effective process?​

Aspect 8 Models and tactics: Design of delivery and intervention models that are fit for purpose, effective, and innovative, based on real attention to how intervention and infrastructure is structured and delivered
Key question - Do we understand what makes a difference on the ground?
Instructions for using the Commissioning Compass system assessment
There are six steps to carrying out the full exercise:
We have said in several places you can go into as much or as little detail as you wish with this assessment.
If you want to have a strategic overview you can just complete steps one and two.
For a more analytical view also do step three.
For the assessment to inform an action or development plan you will need to additionally complete step four and five.
And for the super advanced level step six is for you!
Step One -Getting started
Spend a bit of time familiarising yourself with the 'eight aspects of commissioning.
Understand how the top four are outcomes focused, and systems based and the bottom four are the foundational pillars.
You need to have solid scores on the foundational pillar 'aspects' to be able to effectively move to be aspirational in the top four 'aspects'
Give your place an instinctive score on how you are doing in terms of each of the 'eight aspects'. Do this quickly.  It is just your first pass, your gut reaction.
We will encourage you to revisit this after working through the questions for the aspects.
Scores are categorised as below. Note that scores of 70 and above have been rare in system-assessments so far. ​
0 – 24 Poor (significant risk)​
25 – 49 Fair (lesser/lower risk, improvement required) ​
50 – 74 Good (opportunities identified/issues need to be addressed) ​
75 – 100 Excellent (no action required)​
Instructions for using the Commissioning Compass system assessment
Step Two - self-assessment questions
You will have already recorded a score for each of the eight aspects, based on your initial gut feeling. ​
Next, work through the assessment questions. These are encouraging you to take a deeper look at your system and develop more curiosity. Score your 'system' on each question.

If you are doing this as a team and each person scored individually, do not simply average your results – look at the overall pattern of highs and lows, open up the conversation about what people are seeing in the system to give that score.​

In a workshop, this can be a great way to use appreciative or action enquiry. It will help you to be curious about how stakeholders experience each aspect and what the knock-on impact of that is. This will help too with the next step.
At the end, we’ll compare your initial gut reactions to your actual score.​ Again, we ask you to be curious about where there are differences or alignment. What is that telling you?
If you want to have a more analytical view now move onto step three.
Instructions for using the Commissioning Compass system assessment
Step Three - Factors that constrain and enable
For each aspect, we will explore the factors that constrain or enable you Which hold you/ the system back ? Which most supports you to achieve change and outcomes? ​

Be curious about the depth of your awareness or understanding of each of the factors.  You may wish to explore the factors further before you score them, but this is not essential at this stage.  You can pick that up in your action plan later.
Once you have discussed each of the factors that constrain and enable, select the three most important enablers and the three most important constraints for each of the eight aspects.

If undertaking this assessment with stakeholders, it is likely that there will be very different perspectives in the system. In your workshops, think about how you can explore these perspectives to give you a deeper understanding of your system relationships. There are not right and wrong answers here.  This is to provide you with insight and intelligence to identify where to intervene for the most effective change.

If you want to develop this assessment into an action plan or commissioning development plan we recommend you complete steps four and five. Using your assessment to determine the possible commissioning approaches.
The action plan needs to include all of the insights and actions you have captured along the way in your exploration, curiosity and conversations.
Using your constraints and enablers in an action plan
Step Four - Control and influence. Urgent and important
Once you have evaluated the most enabling and constraining factors for each aspect, you can move to determine what is in your control and what do you need to influence.
Whether the factor is:
in your control
influenceable
out of your control
whether, in the opinion of the group, the factor is:
to be boosted
not to be boosted
would benefit from innovation or experimentation
You can arrive at this by exploring the following questions.
How will we boost the enabling factors in our control?
How can we influence partners and stakeholders for enabling factors out of your control?
For constraining factors within our control, what actions can we take to overcome them?
How will we use our influence where we can, to reduce constraining factors and build on enabling factors?
How will we take account of and work around constraining factors that are not in our control?
What experiments can we run to look at constraining factors that require innovation?
Which of these are the most urgent?
Which of these are the most important?
Which of these would require the most work?
Are there any “quick wins”?
We suggest you use an action plan to capture your actions here. If desired, this action-planning can be developed into a Commissioning Development Plan.
Action-planning on the factors that constrain or enable can help you to expand your ‘elbow room’ - your space and power to make an impact on effective commissioning.

Doing this activity across all eight of the aspects at once is quite a big task.  We suggest you take the bottom four aspects first giving you twenty-four constraints and enablers to work from.  Develop an overall plan for these.  When looking at the top four you may need a separate plan for each.
Introducing the commissioning compass - eight 'approaches' to commissioning
Step Five  - Exploring approaches to commissioning

As you can see from the assessment, we are opening up all of the different ways to assess your strategic commissioning system.  The aspects help you see 'what' the system contains and here we introduce the 'approaches’ to commissioning, which help you assess 'how' to intervene.

You can approach commissioning in different ways, with different methods, different principles, and different means. We have classified this through our eight 'approaches' to commissioning.  Here is a summary of those approaches.
Place-based wellbeing: Design and creation of a place-based wellbeing system.
Leadership of place for whole system change: Creating a system that works.
Unlocking potential: A place where everyone can thrive.
Citizen-centred commissioning: empowering citizens within the system.
Values-based/disruptive commissioning: Changing the status quo
Strategic procurement of services against needs: Services that meet demand
Market management: Creating conditions for best value and outcomes within financial constraints.
Delivery model design: Effective delivery models enabling effective practice.

You can find more detail for each of the 'approaches' within the chapters on 'aspects' of commissioning.  This will allow you to explore in more detail all the options available to you and your system.
Familiarise yourselves with the selected strategic commissioning approach and start to implement it
For each strategic commissioning approach, this includes:
Introducing the approach
How to move towards this approach
What to do, and what not to do, when pursuing this approach
Specific risks to watch out for, including when your room for manoeuvre is limited, and other hints and tips
The commissioning skills and structure that might be needed for this approach
Step Six – Not for the faint hearted!
Now if you are the person at school who always wanted the stretch questions, the advanced level....here is one for you in this assessment.
Once you understand your score on the eight aspects of commissioning, you can use this to select your most appropriate approach to commissioning.
Return now to your scoring for the eight aspects that you did at the beginning.  Add those scores into the table here.
Then read down the table from the top to the bottom
The first score over 50, reading down the table, identifies the recommended strategic commissioning approach.
But critically it must not have a lower score beneath it in the table.
For example -
In this example, the system has been given a mix of scores and you could interpret it several ways.

You might be tempted to focus on approach 2, 'Leadership of the place for whole system change', because it is high up on the table and you have a high score. We would suggest that you don't, because some of the lower down aspects – the ones that are foundational – have weaker scores of below 50. This example is particularly weak in aspect 4 ('citizen, place, and outcome centred' and also has weaknesses in aspects 3 and 6 ('Capacity, capability, and confidence' and 'Making room to make a difference').

In the example, we would suggest that you focus on fixing the foundations which involves focusing on some of the lower down aspects. If you want to pick a single commissioning approach then in this example you would benefit from 'Market management'. If you instead opt for a blend of approaches then consider researching 'market management' and 'Delivery model design' which are both within your grasp and 'strategic procurement of services against needs', and 'values-based/disruptive commissioning' which are both a bit more advanced than your current practice.

In this example the temptation is to go with the 'approach' 2. leadership of place for whole system change.  However, this is undermined by the score on 3.Capacity, capability and confidence and 4. Citizen, place and outcome centred.
The next highest is 5. Information and Insight.  But undermined by 6. Making room to make a difference.
The assessment of your system will help you understand why you have these undermining features and are there quick wins to resolve them, allowing you to move up the approaches for more impact.
Note scores of over 70 are very unusual.  If you do not score over 50 in any aspect then you will need to begin with the foundational aspect of 8. Models and Tactics.
In summary-

An approach higher in the table, is only sustainable if the commissioning aspects lower down the table can support it. They are the foundations.  If the lower aspects are not achieving a high score the risks are higher. It is not impossible to apply a higher approach.  But you need to do it with the awareness that your basics and foundational practice needs boosting, scaffolding or nurturing in the process.

Considering the approaches in this way allows you to critically appraise, or to opt for a blend of approaches, sense-checking your understanding of your challenges, bringing in your insights on your constraints and enablers and any associated action-planning you have developed. A blend of approaches may be useful at different times and in different commissioning situations.

Self-assessment exercise - purpose
This exercise is not about benchmarking or comparison, but about improving:
Our immediate commissioning practice; and
Our ‘room to manoeuvre’ with commissioning –capability, capacity, freedom, power.
To that end, we are evaluating ourselves across services and aspects, then creating a development plan.
Only go into as much detail as you have time for, and is useful!

The Commissioning Self-Assessment
Instructions for the self-assessment
You should have already recorded a score for each of the eight aspects, based on your initial gut feeling.
Now, we are going to work through a longer set of questions. Score your place on each question, but do not simply average your results – look at the overall pattern.
At the end, we’ll compare your initial gut reactions to your actual score.
For each aspect, you will also be presented with a number of factors in place that constrain or enable you as part of the self-assessment.
Which of these factors most holds back your ability to work in this space? Which most supports you?

Think about both your level of understanding of the factors and also the factors themselves. The aspects that hold you back or enable you to work on this aspect of commissioning will be picked up in your commissioning development plan.

Approach 1
Place-based wellbeing
Design and creation of a place-based wellbeing system.
Approach 1: Place-based Wellbeing
Introduction: Focuses on upstream investment in wellbeing and community resilience to reduce demand on care services.
How to move toward: Start by mapping strengths and needs, and build a shared long-term vision with partners.
What to do: Promote co-produced prevention strategies and enable community-led responses.
What not to do: Don’t neglect statutory duties or assume full system redesign is required before progress.
Risks and issues: Vulnerable to short-termism, leadership changes, and funding volatility.
Commissioning skills and structure: Requires communicators who can influence widely, build alliances, and hold the strategic view.

Approach 2
Leadership of place for whole system change
Creating a system that works.
Approach 2: Leadership of Place for Whole System Change
Introduction: Positions the council as a key partner in a shared system, not the central controller, focusing on whole-system impact.
How to move toward: Use shared evidence and cross-organisational learning to build coherent joint working.
What to do: Build trusted relationships, promote co-commissioning, and align vision across partners.
What not to do: Don’t rely on shared plans alone—ensure changes affect frontline practice.
Risks and issues: Can be undermined by weak governance, relationship breakdowns, or overfocus on strategy.
Commissioning skills and structure: Needs senior-level influencing skills, governance literacy, and blended commissioning capabilities.

Approach 3
Unlocking potential

Approach 3: Unlocking potential
Introduction: Aims to build long-term capacity, confidence, and capability in communities to prevent need.
How to move toward: Map formal/informal support, use social value tools, and engage local assets.
What to do: Support micro-providers, community initiatives, and co-production at local level.
What not to do: Don’t expect short-term savings or shift burden onto communities without investment.
Risks and issues: Depends on leadership consistency and maturity of the local voluntary/community sector.
Commissioning skills and structure: Requires strengths in market engagement, community development, and economic analysis.

Approach 4

Approach 4: Citizen-Centred Commissioning
Introduction: Puts the individual in charge of their care and prioritises personal outcomes as success measures.
How to move toward: Develop a compelling shared vision and embed feedback like “Did you get what you needed?”
What to do: Enable co-design, empower personal choice, and align services around lived experience.
What not to do: Avoid tokenistic engagement or overwhelming citizens with too many disconnected choices.
Risks and issues: Risks losing system oversight or statutory compliance if not well-integrated.
Commissioning skills and structure: Requires change agents with high credibility, openness to learning, and system navigation skills.

Approach 5
Values-based/disruptive commissioning
Changing the status quo
Approach 5: Values-Based / Disruptive Commissioning
Introduction: Uses values or innovation to challenge outdated models and promote new solutions.
How to move toward: Start with options appraisal, build commissioner freedom, and learn from outside systems.
What to do: Encourage experimentation, data-led insight, and open collaboration for reform.
What not to do: Don’t pursue perfection or impose innovation without testing in real practice.
Risks and issues: Too much disruption without buy-in risks failure; too little leads to stagnation.
Commissioning skills and structure: Needs creative, data-savvy commissioners with coalition-building and risk-balancing ability.

Approach 6: Strategic Procurement of Services Against Needs
Introduction: Focuses on structured procurement to meet defined needs efficiently and compliantly.
How to move toward: Strengthen procurement-process alignment, market intelligence, and performance monitoring.
What to do: Develop clear specifications based on engagement and evidence, and manage contracts robustly.
What not to do: Avoid focusing only on limitations—procurement should support broader strategic goals.
Risks and issues: Risk of becoming rigid or over-prescriptive; must avoid analysis paralysis.
Commissioning skills and structure: Requires technical procurement, contract management, and analytical capability with service insight.

Approach 7: Market Management
Introduction: Uses commissioning tools to balance cost, resilience, and provider diversity for best value.
How to move toward: Map needs and supply, align procurement strategies, and ensure ongoing engagement.
What to do: Collaborate with providers, manage performance data, and foster innovation.

Risks and issues: Can marginalise co-design or context if dominated by procurement logic.
Commissioning skills and structure: Requires technical strength combined with flexibility, systems thinking, and bridge-building.

Approach 8

Approach 8: Delivery Model Design
Introduction: Focuses on how services are structured and delivered to improve quality and citizen experience.
How to move toward: Engage users, map processes, and learn from service design innovations elsewhere.
What to do: Link design with real practice, co-develop models, and ensure practical implementation.
What not to do: Avoid rolling out untested models or becoming fixated on structure over impact.
Risks and issues: May challenge entrenched interests and stretch delivery capacity if not managed well.
Commissioning skills and structure: Needs design thinkers with operational understanding and credibility across services.
Summing up your score
Have you completed your self-assessment?
The self-assessment is a flexible tool and we suggest that you only use the parts that make sense in your context.
If you do the whole thing then by the end of the workshops you should have done the following:
You have produced an initial ‘gut score’ on how your system performs against all eight aspects.
You have worked your way through each of the eight aspects and worked on the questions. You should have a score out of 100 for each question.

You have worked your way through the ‘factors that constrain and enable’ for each of the eight aspects. For each of the eight aspects, you should have a list of the three most important constraints for your system and the three most important enablers.
If you have completed all of this then your scoring is complete and you can proceed with the next section.

Your scores

Use your scoring table to identify which strategic commissioning approach will provide a best fit for the place, building on local strengths, without letting them to be undermined by weaker aspects. This will not simply be the approach that aligns with the highest scoring aspect.

The first score over 50, reading down the table, which also does not have a lower score beneath it, identifies the recommended strategic commissioning approach. This reflects the fact that an approach higher in the table, whilst being more strengths, system, and outcomes-focused, is only sustainable if the commissioning aspects lower down the table can support it.

Before making the decision whether to select the recommended strategic commissioning approach, or to opt for a blend of approaches, it will be useful to sense-check the suggested strategic commissioning approach with an understanding of specific commissioning challenges, considering key constraints and enablers and any associated action-planning to support the development of local commissioning, and the description of what to consider for this approach. A blend of approaches may be useful at different times and in different commissioning situations.

Using your constraints and enablers in an action plan
For each aspect of commissioning, you should have a list of three key enablers and three key constraints, giving a total of 24 important constraints and 24 important enablers.
Work through these factors and answer identify and record:
Whether the factor is:
in your control
influenceable
out of your control
whether, in the opinion of the group, the factor is:
to be boosted
not to be boosted
would benefit from innovation or experimentation
This will enable you (either with or without partners and other stakeholders) to consider action-planning to support the development of the commissioning function for the place.
Action-planning on the factors that constrain or enable effective commissioning can help you to expand your ‘elbow room’ – yourr space and power to make an impact.

Making space to develop your effectiveness in commissioning will pay dividends in supporting the implementation of the selected strategic commissioning approach and enabling the delivery of strategic commissioning plans.
Familiarise yourselves with the selected strategic commissioning approach and start to implement it

Read or re-visit the pre-reading – Introducing and Implementing Strategic Commissioning Approaches 1-8 to familiarise yourself with the selected strategic commissioning approach(es), to explore and understand the selected approach, to learn what may be required, understand and plan for the associated strategic risks and start to put it into practice (Step 6).  For each strategic commissioning approach, this includes:
Introducing the approach
How to move towards this approach
What to do, and what not to do, when pursuing this approach
Specific risks to watch out for, including when your room for manoeuvre is limited, and other hints and tips
The commissioning skills and structure that might be needed for this approach
The Council may wish to develop a Strategic Commissioning Plan.

The council may wish to articulate the selected strategic commissioning approach in a strategic commissioning plan, which may set medium or long-terms goals for meeting the adult social care needs in the place and how it intends to meet those needs and may also include the intended plans for commissioning development (see Step 5 above) in the place.
Using your constraints and enablers in an action plan
No set format is provided for the action-planning, but we suggest that you could work through some of the following questions to support the development of actions in response to each factor.
How will we boost enabling factors?
For constraining factors within our control, how will we ensure we overcome them?
How will we use our influence where we can, to reduce constraining factors and build on enabling factors?
How will we take account of and work around constraining factors that are not in our control?
What experiments can we run to look at constraining factors that require innovation?
Which of these are the most urgent?
Which of these are the most important?
Which of these would require the most work?
Are there any “quick wins”?
If desired, this action-planning can be developed into a Commissioning Development Plan.
